say.en: India is the world's largest producer of milk, much of it from small farms. Better breeds, better feeding and clean management have multiplied yields in a few decades. In this lesson: Describe dairy farm and poultry farm management.
Compare inbreeding, out-crossing, cross-breeding and interspecific hybridisation.
Explain artificial insemination and MOET.

body.en: *Animal husbandry* is the breeding and care of livestock such as cattle, buffaloes, pigs, sheep, poultry and fish. In dairy farm management, yield depends first on the breed, then on clean, well-ventilated housing, adequate water, good-quality fodder, hygiene during milking and regular veterinary care. In poultry farm management, disease-free and suitable breeds, safe farm conditions, proper feed and water, and hygiene are key; bird flu is a major threat.

points.en: Housing, feed, water and hygiene realise it

say.en: Animal husbandry is the breeding and care of livestock such as cattle, buffaloes, pigs, sheep, poultry and fish. In dairy farm management, yield depends first on the breed, then on clean, well-ventilated housing, adequate water, good-quality fodder, hygiene during milking and regular veterinary care. In poultry farm management, disease-free and suitable breeds, safe farm conditions, proper feed and water, and hygiene are key; bird flu is a major threat. Breed sets the potential yield.
Housing, feed, water and hygiene realise it.
Regular veterinary visits prevent disease.

body.en: A breed is a group of *animals* related by descent and alike in appearance and features. Inbreeding mates closely related animals for 4–6 generations; it increases homozygosity and exposes harmful recessive genes, which selection then removes, but continued inbreeding causes inbreeding depression. Out-crossing mates unrelated animals of the same breed and can relieve that depression. Cross-breeding combines two breeds (Hisardale sheep). Interspecific hybridisation mates two species (a mule from a mare and a donkey). Controlled breeding uses artificial insemination and MOET.

points.en: Inbreeding → homozygosity, then risk of depression
Out-crossing within a breed relieves it
Cross-*breeding*: two breeds; mule: two species

say.en: Press next generation several times. With close inbreeding the heterozygosity bar falls quickly, so harmful recessive alleles show up. One out-cross brings it back up.
Within one breed: close relatives give inbreeding; unrelated animals give out-crossing.
Between breeds: cross-breeding. Between species: interspecific hybridisation, such as the mule.
Controlled breeding: semen of a chosen male is used by artificial insemination; MOET multiplies embryos of an elite cow.

text.en: AI: semen stored frozen, used on many females
MOET: FSH → 6–8 eggs → embryos → surrogate mothers

say.en: Breeding methods at a glance.

problem.en: A farmer keeps a herd of a low-yielding local breed and has bred them among themselves for many generations. Calves are now weak and fewer cows conceive. What has happened, and what should be done?

steps.en: Long inbreeding has raised homozygosity, exposing harmful recessive alleles.
This is inbreeding depression: lower fertility and vigour.
Mating selected animals with unrelated superior animals of the same breed (out-crossing) should restore vigour.
